title: Contraception: Match Effectiveness, Safety, Autonomy, and Preference
bottomLine: Contraceptive counselling is preference-sensitive preventive care. Start with the patient's reproductive goals, desired effectiveness and bleeding profile, contraindications, adherence needs, privacy/access and noncontraceptive benefits; present LARC and short-acting methods without coercion and support the patient's informed choice.
recognize: IUDs and implants provide highly effective reversible contraception without daily adherence.
Condoms/barrier methods remain important for STI risk reduction even when another contraceptive method is used.
differentiate: Estrogen-containing methods have different thrombotic/cardiovascular contraindications from progestin-only and nonhormonal methods.
Emergency contraception is time-sensitive backup, not a substitute for ongoing method planning.
assessment: Ask pregnancy possibility, reproductive timeline, prior method experience, bleeding goals, migraine with aura, VTE/thrombophilia, smoking/age, BP, breast/liver disease, medications/interactions, postpartum/breastfeeding context and STI needs.
workup: Do not require pelvic examination or broad laboratory testing before methods that do not clinically require it; pregnancy assessment is history/test based when uncertainty remains.
management: Offer all medically appropriate methods using shared decision-making and discuss immediate initiation when safe rather than creating unnecessary access barriers.
Use current SOGC/Canadian eligibility guidance for method-specific contraindications and counselling.
medicationSafety: Avoid estrogen-containing contraception when unacceptable thrombotic/stroke risk is present.
Enzyme-inducing medications can reduce effectiveness of selected hormonal methods and require method-specific review.
redFlags: New VTE/stroke symptoms on estrogen-containing method
Severe uncontrolled hypertension where estrogen is being considered
counselling: Use noncoercive language and clarify expected bleeding changes, return-to-fertility expectations and STI protection.
followUp: Follow up for adverse effects or method dissatisfaction and facilitate removal/change promptly when requested.
examTrap: Choosing the method for the patient because it is most effective while ignoring contraindications, values or the patient's request to stop it.
oneLinePearl: The best contraceptive method is medically safe and acceptable enough that the patient wants to use it.
sourceBasis: SOGC contraception guidance and It's a Plan Canadian contraceptive resources

title: Intrauterine Contraception: Safe Insertion, Expected Bleeding, and Complication Recognition
bottomLine: IUC care includes pregnancy/STI risk assessment, informed pain planning, correct insertion technique and counselling about expected bleeding. New severe pain, fever, pregnancy, abnormal strings or heavy bleeding requires evaluation for expulsion, perforation, infection or ectopic pregnancy rather than routine reassurance.
recognize: Copper and levonorgestrel IUCs differ in bleeding effects and noncontraceptive benefits.
Irregular bleeding/cramping is common early; absent strings are a finding requiring localization, not proof of expulsion or perforation.
differentiate: PID risk is concentrated around insertion when an untreated cervical infection is present, but an IUC itself does not cause chronic infection.
Pregnancy with an IUC in place requires early pregnancy-location assessment because ectopic pregnancy must be excluded.
assessment: Assess pregnancy possibility, current pelvic infection symptoms, STI risk/testing needs, uterine/cervical history, bleeding goals, anticoagulation and pain/anxiety preferences.
workup: Use pregnancy testing when indicated and current STI screening based on risk; ultrasound is reserved for difficult insertion, suspected malposition/perforation, missing strings with uncertain location or pregnancy/pain concerns.
management: Use trained insertion technique and individualized analgesia/pain-management options; manage expected bleeding with counselling and current evidence-based options.
Remove promptly when requested and use appropriate localization/referral when removal is difficult or the device is not in the expected position.
medicationSafety: Do not give prophylactic antibiotics routinely solely for IUC insertion without another indication.
Avoid blind instrument retrieval when device location is uncertain.
counselling: Explain expected bleeding, string awareness if desired, expulsion signs and that the patient can request removal at any time.
followUp: Routine mandatory string-check visits are not required for every uncomplicated insertion; reassess symptoms or concerns promptly.
examTrap: Calling absent strings perforation without localizing the device—or insisting the patient continue an IUC they want removed.
oneLinePearl: IUC care is safe placement plus patient-controlled continuation and prompt evaluation of pain, pregnancy or missing location.
sourceBasis: SOGC intrauterine contraception guidance and pain-management statements

title: Contraceptive Implant: Expect Bleeding Variability and Preserve Easy Removal
bottomLine: The etonogestrel implant is highly effective contraception whose most common management issue is unpredictable bleeding. Confirm correct placement, review interacting medications and pregnancy risk, treat troublesome bleeding when appropriate, and remove the implant promptly when requested or when localization/removal requires specialty help.
recognize: Irregular, prolonged, frequent or absent bleeding can all occur and does not by itself mean contraceptive failure.
Deep/nonpalpable implants require localization before attempted removal.
differentiate: New abnormal bleeding still requires pregnancy, infection or structural evaluation when the clinical pattern warrants it; do not attribute everything automatically to the implant.
assessment: Assess bleeding burden, pregnancy possibility, medications including enzyme inducers, insertion site/palpability, patient goals and adverse effects.
workup: Use pregnancy/STI or other AUB workup only when indicated; localize a nonpalpable implant with the appropriate imaging pathway before removal.
management: Reassure expected bleeding when acceptable and use current SOGC management options when bleeding is bothersome.
Remove or replace within the applicable product/evidence interval and respect patient-requested discontinuation without requiring a medical justification.
medicationSafety: Strong hepatic enzyme inducers can reduce contraceptive effectiveness and require interaction-specific counselling or method change.
Do not perform blind deep removal attempts because neurovascular injury can occur.
counselling: Set expectations about unpredictable bleeding before insertion and explain that removal remains available whenever desired.
followUp: Review bothersome bleeding, interaction changes or localization concerns rather than scheduling unnecessary routine visits.
examTrap: Calling irregular implant bleeding dangerous without evaluating severity—or refusing removal because the implant remains effective.
oneLinePearl: Implant bleeding is often unpredictable; patient autonomy and safe removal are part of the method.
sourceBasis: SOGC 2025 contraceptive implant removal position statement

title: Oral Contraceptives: Screen Estrogen Risk and Make Adherence Realistic
bottomLine: Combined oral contraception requires BP and estrogen-risk assessment, while progestin-only pills have different adherence and safety profiles. Choose the formulation for patient priorities and contraindications, counsel missed-pill rules and interactions, and avoid unnecessary pelvic exams/labs that create access barriers.
recognize: Combined pills can improve cycle control/dysmenorrhea/acne but add estrogen-related VTE/stroke risk.
Progestin-only options may be preferred when estrogen is contraindicated.
differentiate: Migraine with aura, current/high VTE risk, severe hypertension and selected smoking/age contexts can make estrogen unacceptable.
A history of uncomplicated migraine without aura is not the same risk category.
assessment: Check BP and ask migraine aura, smoking, VTE/thrombophilia, cardiovascular disease, postpartum/breastfeeding status, liver/breast disease, medications and adherence preferences.
workup: Routine pelvic examination, Pap/HPV screening or thrombophilia testing is not required solely to prescribe oral contraception unless independently indicated.
management: Select combined or progestin-only formulation based on eligibility, bleeding goals and adherence; provide clear start and missed-pill/backup instructions using current product/SOGC guidance.
medicationSafety: Review enzyme-inducing drugs and selected anticonvulsants; educate about VTE/stroke symptoms for estrogen-containing methods.
Do not use estrogen-containing contraception solely to 'regularize' bleeding before evaluating unexplained concerning AUB.
redFlags: Chest pain/dyspnea/leg swelling concerning for VTE
counselling: Discuss expected breakthrough bleeding, adherence strategy and STI protection separately.
followUp: Recheck BP and tolerability after initiation as clinically appropriate; adjust method when adverse effects or adherence barriers persist.
examTrap: Requiring a pelvic exam before prescribing the pill or giving estrogen to a patient with migraine with aura without risk review.
oneLinePearl: For oral contraception, BP, estrogen risk, interactions and adherence matter more than a pelvic exam.
sourceBasis: SOGC contraception guidance and Canadian contraceptive resources

title: Emergency Contraception: A Time-Sensitive Choice, Then an Ongoing Plan
bottomLine: Emergency contraception works best when provided promptly. Choose copper IUC, ulipristal or levonorgestrel according to timing, effectiveness, BMI/weight considerations, drug interactions, ongoing contraception plans and patient preference; then address STI risk and transition to reliable ongoing contraception.
recognize: Copper IUC is the most effective EC and provides ongoing contraception when medically appropriate.
Ulipristal retains efficacy later in the five-day window better than levonorgestrel and can be affected by subsequent progestin timing.
differentiate: EC prevents pregnancy before establishment; it does not terminate an established pregnancy.
A late menstrual period or pregnancy symptoms require pregnancy evaluation rather than repeated EC alone.
assessment: Determine intercourse timing, cycle/pregnancy possibility, prior unprotected episodes, current contraception, enzyme-inducing drugs, BMI/weight context, STI risk and IUC eligibility/preferences.
workup: Do not delay oral EC for pregnancy testing when a current pregnancy from the recent exposure is biologically impossible; test when an earlier pregnancy is plausible or menses are delayed.
management: Offer the most effective acceptable option as soon as possible and provide method-specific instructions for starting/resuming ongoing contraception after EC.
Arrange copper-IUC insertion urgently when chosen/eligible and local access allows.
medicationSafety: Strong enzyme inducers can reduce oral EC efficacy; copper IUC may be preferred when appropriate.
After ulipristal, starting progestin too soon can reduce its effect; follow current Canadian product/SOGC timing guidance.
redFlags: Severe pelvic pain/syncope with pregnancy possibility
Delayed menses or persistent pregnancy symptoms after EC
counselling: Explain expected menstrual timing changes, pregnancy testing timing, STI testing and that EC does not harm an established pregnancy if it fails.
followUp: Confirm ongoing contraceptive plan and pregnancy test if the next period is significantly delayed or symptoms develop.
examTrap: Refusing EC because the patient is near presumed ovulation or delaying treatment while waiting for unnecessary tests.
oneLinePearl: Emergency contraception is a clock—offer the most effective acceptable method now, then plan what comes next.
sourceBasis: SOGC It's a Plan emergency contraception resource

title: Preconception Care: Optimize Health Before Early Pregnancy Physiology Starts
bottomLine: Preconception care identifies modifiable medication, nutrition, chronic-disease, infection, genetic and social risks before pregnancy recognition. Review folic acid needs, immunization, teratogens, diabetes/BP/thyroid control, substance use, fertility timing and patient goals without making pregnancy contingent on perfect health.
recognize: Early organ development occurs before many pregnancies are recognized, so medication and folate review should occur before conception when possible.
differentiate: Preconception counselling supports informed risk reduction; it is not a requirement to obtain permission to become pregnant.
assessment: Review chronic disease, medications/supplements, pregnancy history, immunizations, nutrition, folate risk, smoking/alcohol/substances, infectious/genetic/family history, mental health, IPV, occupational exposures and fertility goals/age.
workup: Order condition/risk-specific testing rather than a universal preconception panel; ensure cervical/STI/genetic carrier testing follows current indications and ancestry/family history rather than assumptions.
management: Optimize chronic disease and replace contraindicated/teratogenic drugs with safer effective alternatives when feasible; recommend folic acid/multivitamin supplementation according to SOGC risk guidance.
Update indicated immunizations before pregnancy when live vaccines or timing matter.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop essential psychiatric, antiseizure or other chronic medication solely because pregnancy is planned; balance disease relapse and fetal risks with specialist input where needed.
redFlags: Current teratogenic exposure requiring urgent review
counselling: Discuss fertility decline with age accurately without coercion, and address nutrition/activity in nonstigmatizing language.
followUp: Close medication/immunization/referral actions and transition promptly to prenatal care once pregnant.
examTrap: Telling a patient to stop an effective chronic medication immediately before pregnancy without weighing disease risk or arranging a safer plan.
oneLinePearl: Preconception care reduces avoidable risk before the pregnancy test turns positive.

title: Infertility: Evaluate Ovulation, Tubes/Uterus, and Sperm in Parallel
bottomLine: Infertility evaluation should not focus only on the person who may ovulate. Assess ovulatory function, uterine/tubal factors and semen in parallel, and start earlier when age or known risk makes delay costly. Refer promptly when diminished ovarian reserve, severe male factor, tubal disease or complex endocrinology is likely.
recognize: Irregular/absent menses suggests ovulatory dysfunction; prior PID/ectopic/endometriosis/surgery raises tubal risk; male-factor infertility is common and needs early semen evaluation.
differentiate: Infertility is not diagnosed solely from an AMH value, and ovarian reserve testing does not directly measure spontaneous fertility in every patient.
assessment: Review duration/frequency/timing of intercourse or insemination, cycle pattern, pregnancy history, STI/PID/endometriosis/surgery, medications, sexual function, age and both partners' reproductive history when applicable.
workup: Use ovulation assessment when uncertain, semen analysis early and uterine/tubal evaluation according to history; endocrine tests are targeted to cycle/symptom clues.
Do not order broad thrombophilia/immune panels as routine infertility screening.
management: Treat reversible causes, optimize preconception health and refer to fertility care based on age/duration and identified factors rather than waiting for every low-yield test.
medicationSafety: Ovulation-induction drugs carry multiple-gestation and ovarian-hyperstimulation risks and require appropriate monitoring/specialty protocols.
redFlags: Very abnormal semen analysis or suspected gonadal failure
counselling: Use inclusive language about partners and pathways to pregnancy; explain that infertility commonly involves factors from more than one domain.
followUp: Ensure parallel investigations are completed and referrals are not delayed by sequential low-value testing.
examTrap: Completing an extensive female workup before obtaining a semen analysis.
oneLinePearl: Infertility workup runs in parallel: ovulation, anatomy and sperm.
sourceBasis: SOGC fertility and advanced reproductive age guidance

title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: Stabilize, Exclude Pregnancy, Then Use the Pattern
bottomLine: AUB evaluation starts with hemodynamic stability and pregnancy exclusion, then uses bleeding pattern, anemia risk and PALM-COEIN structural/nonstructural causes. Endometrial sampling is risk-based—not performed on everyone and not omitted when age/risk or persistent abnormal bleeding makes malignancy plausible.
recognize: Heavy/prolonged/irregular/intermenstrual bleeding can result from structural lesions, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial/coagulopathic causes, medications or pregnancy-related disease.
differentiate: Postmenopausal bleeding is not routine premenopausal AUB and requires an endometrial-cancer pathway.
Bleeding in pregnancy requires ectopic/miscarriage/obstetric assessment rather than a chronic AUB algorithm.
assessment: Assess stability, pregnancy possibility, bleeding quantity/trajectory, anemia symptoms, cycle pattern, medications/anticoagulants, endocrine/coagulopathy features and endometrial-cancer risk.
workup: Pregnancy test and CBC are core when applicable; use TSH/coagulation/iron studies selectively and pelvic ultrasound when structural disease is plausible.
Endometrial sampling is based on age/risk/persistent bleeding and local guideline criteria rather than a universal cutoff alone.
management: Acute unstable heavy bleeding requires emergency stabilization and gynecologic management.
Stable treatment is cause- and goal-specific and may include LNG-IUS, hormonal therapy, tranexamic acid/NSAIDs or structural intervention.
medicationSafety: Estrogen-containing treatment requires VTE/cardiovascular contraindication review; tranexamic-acid decisions require thrombosis-context assessment.
redFlags: Persistent intermenstrual bleeding or malignancy risk
counselling: Explain that treatment depends on both cause and goals for contraception/fertility/bleeding control.
followUp: Document response, hemoglobin/iron recovery and completion of imaging/biopsy when indicated.
examTrap: Treating heavy bleeding hormonally without checking pregnancy or malignancy risk—or biopsying every young patient without risk assessment.
oneLinePearl: AUB is stability, pregnancy, pattern and cancer risk before treatment choice.

title: Dysmenorrhea: Primary Pain or Secondary Pelvic Disease?
bottomLine: Primary dysmenorrhea is cyclic prostaglandin-mediated pain with otherwise reassuring history/exam. Progressive pain, dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, infertility, pelvic mass or poor response to adequate NSAID/hormonal therapy raises secondary causes such as endometriosis, adenomyosis or fibroids.
recognize: Primary dysmenorrhea typically begins around menses and improves after the first days of flow; adolescents often have no pelvic pathology.
differentiate: Endometriosis, adenomyosis, PID, fibroids, ovarian pathology and obstructive anomalies cause secondary pain patterns.
assessment: Ask onset relative to menarche, cyclicity, bleeding, bowel/bladder symptoms, dyspareunia, fertility goals, sexual history/PID risk and response to prior therapy.
workup: No routine imaging is required for a classic primary pattern; pelvic ultrasound and further evaluation are used when secondary disease is suspected or treatment fails.
management: Use scheduled NSAID therapy started before/at symptom onset when safe and offer hormonal suppression according to contraceptive preference/eligibility.
Refer suspected endometriosis or structural disease when persistent/refractory or fertility concerns warrant it.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs require GI/renal/CV risk review; hormonal therapy requires method-specific contraindication assessment.
redFlags: Progressive pain with abnormal bleeding or infertility
counselling: Validate pain and explain that severe recurrent menstrual pain is treatable and should not be normalized when function is impaired.
followUp: Reassess after an adequate therapeutic trial and investigate secondary causes when expected improvement does not occur.
examTrap: Telling an adolescent severe disabling pain is normal without offering treatment or reassessing failure of first-line therapy.
oneLinePearl: Primary dysmenorrhea should respond to prostaglandin suppression; failure makes you look for a secondary cause.
sourceBasis: SOGC endometriosis/chronic pelvic pain and gynecology resources
